On keeping a small garden

A garden the size of a dining table teaches more than a field does. Every decision is visible from the kitchen window, and every mistake has a name. This essay collects what a few seasons of very small-scale growing taught me about patience, soil, and the odd pleasure of watching something you did not plan turn out well.

Start with the soil

Most advice begins with seeds, and most failures begin with soil. A pot of tired compost will grow a tired plant no matter how carefully it is watered. Before buying anything, dig a hand's depth and look: is it dark and crumbly, or pale and packed like flour? Squeeze a fistful. If it holds a shape and then falls apart at a poke, you are in better shape than most.

The simplest test needs nothing but a jar. Fill it a third with earth, top it up with water, shake it, and leave it overnight. Sand settles first, silt next, and clay hangs in the water for days. The proportions tell you what to add, and how much, and what to avoid adding at all.

What to add

  • Compost, in thin layers, every autumn.
  • Leaf mould for water retention, if your soil is sandy.
  • Coarse grit, not sand, if your soil is heavy clay.
  • Nothing at all, for a season, if the plants are already thriving.

What to leave out

  1. Fresh manure, which burns roots.
  2. Peat, which is better left in the ground.
  3. Anything you cannot identify.

Choose plants that forgive

Beginners are often told to grow tomatoes. Tomatoes are a fine plant, but they punish neglect with a sullen sort of disappointment. Radishes, by contrast, are ready in a month and tolerate nearly everything. Lettuce, chard, and herbs such as mint, chives and parsley form a sensible first list.

The first year, plant what you will actually eat. The second year, plant what surprises you. By the third you will have worked out which is which.

That quotation is not from anyone famous; it is what a neighbour said over the fence while I stared at a failed bed of carrots. She was right, and she was also holding a basket of better carrots than mine.

A weekly routine

Gardens reward routine more than effort. Ten minutes on the same morning each week beats a heroic Sunday every other month. A plain schedule looks like this:

Monday
Water the pots, check the undersides of leaves for aphids.
Thursday
Pick whatever is ready, pinch back the basil, pull a few weeds.
Sunday
Turn the compost, note anything strange in the notebook.

Tools worth owning

You need fewer tools than catalogues suggest. A hand trowel, a pair of snips, a watering can with a fine rose and a kneeling pad cover nearly every task. For the rest, borrow from a neighbour and return it cleaner than you found it.

  radishes   sown  3 May   up  9 May
  chard      sown  3 May   up 12 May
  mint       potted        thriving, too much
